solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Run from large snake (6)

blocks.note: L is the size label for large, as on clothing
the adder is Britain's one venomous snake

annotation.surface: Fleeing in terror from a big snake.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Run' reads as a verb telling you to flee, but it is a noun: the line of undone stitches in a pair of tights.
annotation.definitionFit: A ladder in tights or stockings is what Americans call a run: a vertical line where the knit has come undone.

entries.clue: Defence of Area 51 not straight (5)

blocks.note: A is the standard abbreviation for area
51 in Roman numerals is L (50) plus I (1)
bi, short for bisexual, is the opposite of straight

annotation.surface: A cover story for the secret American base at Area 51 that doesn't quite add up.
annotation.walkthrough: Area 51 looks like one proper name, but it splits into a word and a number, and the number is read in Roman numerals.
annotation.definitionFit: An alibi is the defence that the accused was somewhere else when the crime was committed.

entries.clue: Obstruct American act in part of Middle Eastern city (9)

blocks.note: to dam a river is to block its flow
A is a standard abbreviation for American
a play's acts are divided into scenes, so a scene is part of an act

annotation.surface: A US operation blocking a play being staged in some quarter of a Middle Eastern city.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In part' belongs to the wordplay, not the definition: a scene is an act in part. The definition is 'of Middle Eastern city', an adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: Damascene means of or from Damascus, the Syrian capital, as in Damascene steel or a Damascene conversion.

entries.clue: Suggestive question stops salary increase (6)

indicatorNotes.stops: To stop a hole is to plug it, so the question goes into the gap inside the other word.

blocks.note: a rise is a British pay increase; Americans say raise
QU is a standard abbreviation for question

annotation.surface: An awkward question that halts a pay rise.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Suggestive question' reads as one phrase, but 'Suggestive' is the definition on its own.
annotation.definitionFit: A risqué joke is slightly indecent, suggestive rather than openly rude.

entries.clue: Left family member’s nursing home (8)

indicatorNotes.nursing: To nurse something is to hold it close, so one word holds the other inside it.

blocks.note: a sister is a family member; the 's means 'is', joining it to 'nursing'
to be in is to be at home

annotation.surface: Someone has gone away, and the relative who stayed behind is caring for the house.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Left' reads as a verb, someone departing, but it is the heraldic sense of the answer. With 'sister' in the clue, a nurse is also a ward sister, which helps the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: Sinister is Latin for left, and in heraldry it still means the left side of a shield as the bearer holds it.

entries.clue: Eyes parcel, livid about courier service (7,8)

indicatorNotes.about: Letters that are turned about are moved around, so the fodder is rearranged.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 15 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Someone eyes a parcel, furious about how the delivery firm has handled it.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface is about a delivery going wrong, which is why the fodder hides so well: the answer is the service itself.
annotation.definitionFit: Special Delivery is the Royal Mail's guaranteed next-day service, one kind of courier service.

entries.clue: Origin of new carbon-free business (8)

indicatorNotes.free: Something carbon-free has had its carbon taken out, so the letter C is removed.

blocks.note: N is a standard abbreviation for new
business in the sense of goings-on, as in 'a lot of business at the port'
C is the chemical symbol for carbon, and it is the letter taken away

annotation.surface: Where a new green company came from.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Carbon-free business' sounds like a net-zero start-up, but the hyphen hides an instruction: take C out of ACTIVITY.
annotation.definitionFit: Nativity means birth, a thing's origin, as in someone's place of nativity.

entries.clue: This person informed nurses taking legal action (5)

indicatorNotes.nurses: To nurse something is to hold it close, so one word holds the other inside it.

blocks.note: in criminal slang to sing is to inform on others, so sung means informed
'this person' is the setter talking about themselves: I

annotation.surface: Someone who blew the whistle is looking after people who are going to court.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Informed' is not about knowledge but about grassing: a criminal who informs sings to the police.
annotation.definitionFit: To sue is to take legal action against someone, so suing is taking legal action.

entries.clue: Support shut up about old United manager in the end (9)

indicatorNotes.about: To go about something is to surround it, so one word wraps around the others.
indicatorNotes.in the end: Only the end of the manager counts, which is its last letter.

blocks.note: to encage something is to shut it up in a cage
O is a standard abbreviation for old
U is a standard abbreviation for United, as in football club names
the last letter of manager

annotation.surface: A football fan telling critics to be quiet and back the former Manchester United manager.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old United manager' calls up Alex Ferguson, but it is three separate pieces: O, U and the end of manager.
annotation.definitionFit: To support someone and to encourage them are the same thing: giving them backing and confidence.

entries.clue: During trial it must establish critical indicator of success (6,4)

indicatorNotes.During: What goes on during a stretch of words sits inside them, so the answer is spelt out within the run of letters.

blocks.note: hidden in triaL IT MUST ESTablish

annotation.surface: In any trial, this is the point that must be proved to win.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer runs across four words, starting at the last letter of 'trial'.
annotation.definitionFit: A litmus test is a single decisive check whose result settles the question, named after the paper that shows acid or alkali.

entries.clue: Bird missing front bit of foot (4)

indicatorNotes.missing front: A word missing its front has lost its first letter.

blocks.note: the finch is a small seed-eating bird
F is the front letter of finch, and it is the one dropped

annotation.surface: A bird that has lost the front of its foot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Foot' sits beside 'Bird' and reads as a claw, but it is the unit of length: twelve inches make a foot.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by measurement: twelve of these imperial units make up a foot, so one of them is a literal fraction of it.

entries.clue: State failure over university essentially buried (8)

indicatorNotes.essentially: The essence of a word is its core, so only its middle letters are taken.

blocks.note: a miss is a failed attempt
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over
U is a standard abbreviation for university
the middle two letters of buRIed

annotation.surface: A failing university quietly swept under the carpet by the state.
annotation.walkthrough: 'State' reads as a verb, to declare, but it is the noun: one of the fifty US states.
annotation.definitionFit: Missouri is a US state in the Midwest, named after the river that runs through it.

entries.clue: Relax earl beset by very painful condition (3,3)

indicatorNotes.beset by: Something beset by others is surrounded by them, so the earl sits between the two pieces that follow.

blocks.note: V is a standard abbreviation for very
E is an abbreviation for earl
gout is a painful swelling of the joints, classically the big toe

annotation.surface: A nobleman in agony from his gout is told to take it easy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Very painful condition' reads as one phrase, but 'very' is its own letter, and the earl is hemmed in between it and the illness. Gout is the rich old aristocrat's disease of cartoons.
annotation.definitionFit: To veg out is to relax completely, sitting as inert as a vegetable.

entries.clue: Writer’s guild met periodically (4)

indicatorNotes.periodically: Something done periodically happens at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken.

blocks.note: every other letter of these two words, starting from the first

annotation.surface: An authors' society that gathers every so often.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Writer's guild' reads as one body, but the 's is 'is', splitting the definition from the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: André Gide was a French novelist and Nobel laureate, author of The Immoralist.

entries.clue: Check that line’s removed from copy (9)

indicatorNotes.removed from: A letter removed from a word is taken out of it.

blocks.note: a limitation is a check or restriction
L is a standard abbreviation for line, and it is the letter taken out; the 's is 'is'

annotation.surface: A proofreader making sure a line has been cut from the text.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Check' looks like an instruction to verify, but it is a noun meaning a restraint, and 'copy' is not text for printing but a fake.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a fake that reproduces an original, whether a painting or a voice, is both an imitation and a copy.

entries.clue: Protestant man hared after boor, dropping ring (8)

indicatorNotes.after: What comes after something is placed behind it, so the man running follows the boor.
indicatorNotes.dropping: To drop something is to let it go, so the ring-shaped letter is removed.

blocks.note: a lout is an uncouth, rowdy man
the letter O is ring-shaped, and it is the one dropped from LOUT
a man is a he
to hare is to run fast, so hared means ran

annotation.surface: A man sprints after a thug who has let go of a ring he snatched.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Protestant man' reads as one description, but 'man' belongs to the wordplay as HE, and 'hared' has to be read in the past tense as RAN.
annotation.definitionFit: Lutherans belong to the Protestant church founded on Martin Luther's teaching.

entries.clue: Improving the quality of river feature restricting current in England (9)

indicatorNotes.restricting: To restrict something is to hem it in, so the river and the feature close around the current.
indicatorNotes.in: Everything so far is put in the abbreviation for England.

blocks.note: R is a standard abbreviation for river
I is the physics symbol for electric current
the chin is a facial feature
ENG is the abbreviation for England

annotation.surface: A way of improving a river landscape by holding back its flow somewhere in England.
annotation.walkthrough: 'River feature' reads as one thing, a weir or meander, but it is R and a facial feature, and I sits between them before the whole lot goes inside ENG.
annotation.definitionFit: To enrich something is to improve its quality, as when soil is enriched with compost.

entries.clue: Prevent vicar regularly touring topless bar in unsightly development (8)

indicatorNotes.regularly: Taken regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of vicar is used.
indicatorNotes.touring: To tour a place is to go round it, so STOP goes round the bar.
indicatorNotes.topless: A word written down the page has its top at the start, so the first letter goes.

blocks.note: to stop something is to prevent it
a pub is a bar; topless, it loses its P to leave UB
the second and fourth letters of vIcAr

annotation.surface: Stopping the local vicar from visiting a topless bar in some ugly new housing estate.
annotation.walkthrough: SUBTOPIA is a British coinage from suburb plus utopia. The vicar's letters come last, after STOP has gone round the bar.
annotation.definitionFit: Subtopia is a pejorative word for sprawling, characterless suburban development spoiling the landscape.

entries.clue: Anxious to have son in the lead for cushy job (8)

indicatorNotes.in the lead: To be in the lead is to be at the front, so the son's letter moves to the start of the word.

blocks.note: S is a standard abbreviation for son; it is lifted out of the anxious word and put first
INSECURE means anxious and unsure; this is what is left once its S moves to the front

annotation.surface: A worried parent wants their son to be top of the list for an easy job.
annotation.walkthrough: The S is already in INSECURE; the clue asks you to move it from third place to the front, not to add another.
annotation.definitionFit: A sinecure is a post that pays but demands little or no work, the very definition of a cushy job.

entries.clue: Dance with heretic, but not bishop (4)

indicatorNotes.but not: Heretic but not bishop means the heretic with the bishop taken away.

blocks.note: a heretic rebels against church doctrine
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop, and it is the letter taken out

annotation.surface: Dancing with a heretic is fine, so long as the bishop isn't involved.
annotation.walkthrough: The church words make the surface feel ecclesiastical; REBEL is a looser synonym for heretic, a dissenter against authority.
annotation.definitionFit: A reel is a lively Scottish or Irish folk dance.

entries.clue: In flipping wellies, bafflingly descend with control (6)

indicatorNotes.In: What is in a stretch of words sits inside them, so the answer is spelt out within the run of letters.
indicatorNotes.flipping: Something flipped is turned over, so the hidden letters are read backwards.

blocks.note: hidden in welLIES BAfflingly

annotation.surface: Someone tries to climb down a rock face in wellington boots, to general bewilderment.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British swear word for the wellies, but it is the reversal instruction. Wellies are rubber wellington boots.
annotation.definitionFit: To abseil is to descend a rope in a controlled way, braking as you go.

entries.clue: Party to put back election (6)

indicatorNotes.put back: Something put back is sent the other way, so TO is written backwards.

blocks.note: a ball is a formal dancing party
used as it stands

annotation.surface: A political party trying to postpone a vote.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Party' and 'election' make it all politics, but the party is a dance and 'put back' turns 'to' round rather than delaying anything.
annotation.definitionFit: A ballot is a vote, and by extension an election decided by one.

entries.clue: Thin and tense, had a rest (5)

blocks.note: lean means thin, with no spare fat
T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

annotation.surface: Someone skinny and stressed finally took a break.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Had a rest' reads as took a break, but here it means propped oneself: the ladder had a rest against the wall, it leant there.
annotation.definitionFit: To lean on something is to rest against it, so leant means rested or had a rest.

entries.clue: Foolish European climber nearly slipping on ice at first (8)

indicatorNotes.nearly: Nearly a word is the word not quite finished, so its last letter goes.
indicatorNotes.slipping: Letters that slip move out of place, so the pieces are rearranged.
indicatorNotes.at first: Only the first letter of ice is taken.

blocks.note: E is a standard abbreviation for European
climber nearly, without its last letter
the first letter of ice

annotation.surface: A reckless European mountaineer nearly falls on the ice.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Climber' looks like it wants a synonym such as a vine, but the word itself is the fodder, cut short by one letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Imbecile can be an adjective meaning stupid or foolish, as in an imbecile remark.

entries.clue: Continue to sleep with porky Italian on vacation (3,2)

indicatorNotes.on vacation: A vacated word has been emptied, so only its outer letters are left.

blocks.note: porky is short for porky pie, Cockney rhyming slang for a lie
the outer letters of ItaliaN

annotation.surface: Staying in bed with a plump Italian while on holiday.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Porky' looks like it describes the Italian's weight, but it is a noun: porky pie is rhyming slang for lie.
annotation.definitionFit: To lie in is to stay in bed later than usual, continuing to sleep.

entries.clue: Distinguished singer against plugging charity, having retired (4)

indicatorNotes.plugging: A plug fills a hole, so the V goes inside AID.
indicatorNotes.having retired: To retire is to draw back, so the whole combination is written backwards.

blocks.note: aid is charitable help, as in Live Aid
v for versus, meaning against

annotation.surface: A famous singer who once campaigned against a charity and has since stepped back from public life.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Retired' fits a singer leaving the stage so well that it is easy to miss as the instruction to turn the letters round.
annotation.definitionFit: A diva is a celebrated female opera singer, a prima donna.

entries.clue: Quietly looking embarrassed, journalist accepts penalty set in advance (10)

indicatorNotes.accepts: To accept something is to take it in, so ED takes FINE inside.

blocks.note: p for piano, the musical direction for quietly
an embarrassed face goes red
ED, short for editor, is the crossword's standard journalist
a fine is a money penalty

annotation.surface: A red-faced reporter quietly pays a fine that was fixed before the hearing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Quietly' reads as an adverb for how the journalist behaves, but it is the musical direction piano, so it gives a single letter. The penalty goes inside the journalist's two letters, not after them.
annotation.definitionFit: Predefined means defined or set in advance, like predefined settings on a device.

entries.clue: Possibly heading for a fall, not prepared to make king saint (8)

indicatorNotes.to make: To make one thing another is to turn it into the other, so the king becomes a saint.

blocks.note: unready means not prepared
R for rex, Latin for king, and it is the letter swapped out
ST is the abbreviation for saint, and it goes where R was

annotation.surface: An unready monarch being made a saint may well be heading for a fall.
annotation.walkthrough: Æthelred the Unready was an English king, which makes 'not prepared' and 'king' feel like one story.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone unsteady on their feet may well be about to fall, which is why the definition carries 'possibly'.

entries.clue: Popular story remaining unverified on purpose (6)

blocks.note: in cricket the leg side of the field is also called the on side
an end is an aim or purpose, as in 'to that end'

annotation.surface: A widely told tale that no one has ever confirmed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On purpose' reads as deliberately, but it splits in two. The leg or on side is the half of a cricket field behind the batsman's legs.
annotation.definitionFit: A legend is a popular traditional story that is widely believed but has never been proved true.
